title: Artificial intelligence and biosecurity: capabilities, threat pathways, and defense-in-depth governance
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 14 Sep 2026]
    Title:Artificial intelligence and biosecurity: capabilities, threat pathways, and defense-in-depth governance
View PDF
            Abstract:Artificial intelligence is reshaping biological research across an increasingly connected digital-to-physical workflow. General-purpose large language models can retrieve and integrate scientific information, support experimental planning, and computational analysis; biological foundation models can predict, optimize, and generate proteins, genes, and genome-scale sequences; agentic systems can coordinate multistep research tasks; automated laboratories can partially close the design-build-test-learn cycle. These technologies could greatly benefit medicine, public health, and biotechnology. However, their biosecurity risk depends not only on what the AI can do, but also on who uses it, their expertise and intent, their access to laboratory tools and materials, and the safeguards in place. Current evidence shows that AI uplift exists but primarily affects digital rather than physical tasks. Frontier systems have exceeded expert baselines on in-silico, and screening-evasion benchmarks, whereas controlled wet-laboratory studies find that tacit knowledge and physical execution remain substantial barriers. This review describes the different biological threats from AI tool use, from information gathering and biological design to procurement, synthesis, testing, scale-up, and potential release. We further examine why alignment techniques for general-purpose models transfer poorly to biological ones, and the emerging role of interpretability in auditing whether hazardous capabilities are genuinely removed. We argue for defense-in-depth governance that links capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem, reducing high-consequence risk while preserving beneficial use.

report.summary: A new review argues AI boosts biosecurity risks mainly in digital design, while physical lab barriers persist, requiring layered governance tied to capability thresholds.
report.background: AI is increasingly embedded in biology, from large language models that synthesize literature and plan experiments to biological foundation models that design proteins and genomes, agentic systems that coordinate research, and automated labs that close the design-build-test-learn loop. These advances promise faster drug discovery, diagnostics, and biotechnology. But they also create dual-use risks: the same tools could help malicious actors gather information, design dangerous biological agents, evade screening, or scale production. Prior biosecurity debates focused on DNA synthesis and gain-of-function research; now general-purpose and biological AI add new pathways. The review notes that risk depends on actor expertise, intent, lab access, and safeguards, not only model capability. Evidence suggests AI uplift is real but concentrated in digital tasks, while wet-lab barriers remain.
key_points: AI now spans the biological workflow: LLMs retrieve and integrate scientific information and support experimental planning; biological foundation models predict, optimize, and generate proteins, genes, and genome-scale sequences; agentic systems coordinate multistep tasks; and automated laboratories partially close the design-build-test-learn cycle.

Biosecurity risk is not determined by model capability alone. It also depends on who uses the system, their expertise and intent, their access to laboratory tools and materials, and the safeguards in place. Governance must therefore target actors, access points, and workflows, not just AI models.

Current evidence shows AI uplift exists but is primarily digital. Frontier systems have exceeded expert baselines on in-silico tasks and screening-evasion benchmarks, while controlled wet-lab studies find that tacit knowledge and physical execution remain substantial barriers to misuse.

Alignment techniques for general-purpose models transfer poorly to biological models. This makes standard safety tuning insufficient for biological risk, and interpretability is emerging as a way to audit whether hazardous capabilities have genuinely been removed rather than merely suppressed.

The authors argue for defense-in-depth governance: link capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem, including model developers, cloud providers, synthesis firms, labs, and funders, to reduce high-consequence risk while preserving beneficial use.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the review signals that biosecurity will become a core evaluation and compliance domain, not a niche concern. Model developers may face capability thresholds, gated access, screening requirements, and audits, especially for biological foundation models and agentic systems. Interpretability and red-teaming tools will matter for proving that dangerous capabilities are removed. For developers, integrating biosecurity checks into agent pipelines and lab-automation APIs could become standard. For regular users, medical and biotech benefits should continue, but access to high-risk biological design features may be restricted, verified, or monitored. The overall shift is from voluntary principles toward layered, risk-proportionate governance across the digital-to-physical pipeline.
report.tools: Related tools to watch include AlphaFold and ESM/ESMFold for protein structure and sequence modeling, RFdiffusion and ProteinMPNN for protein design, and SecureDNA or IGSC synthesis-screening standards for DNA procurement. For evaluation and governance, Inspect, HELM, and biosecurity red-teaming frameworks from NTI Bio and Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security are useful references. Open-source agent frameworks and lab-automation platforms should be monitored for built-in biosecurity controls.
